opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say we're at a stage where it works surprisingly well in many cases, but it's not yet something I'd call "solved."

Group photos are much harder than a single object or a single person. With one person you have a clear subject, and the model can focus its capacity on getting the face, the clothing and the pose right. With a group you have occlusion: someone's arm is behind someone else's shoulder, people overlap, and the back of the scene is completely invisible. The system has to hallucinate plausible geometry for everything the camera didn't see, and it also has to keep each person's identity consistent. When you print it out as a little figurine, people are very sensitive to faces. If your friend's face looks slightly off, the whole thing feels wrong, even if the geometry is technically fine.

Printability adds another layer. A 3D model that looks good on screen isn't necessarily printable. You need watertight meshes, reasonable wall thickness, no tiny floating parts, and a base that lets the thing stand up. Thin features like fingers or hair strands can break easily. So beyond generation quality, a lot of our engineering effort goes into making the output something you can actually send to a printer, and have it come out in one piece.

So where are we? For simple groups, say two or three people standing fairly close together with a clean background, the results are often good enough that people are genuinely delighted. That's the kind of thing you'd give as a gift for a wedding or a family reunion. For larger groups, complex poses, or heavy occlusion, there's still visible room for improvement, and sometimes users need a few tries or a bit of manual cleanup.

But the trend is what excites me. Every few months the quality jumps noticeably. Coming from a graphics and simulation background, I used to think producing this kind of asset would always need a skilled artist and many hours of work. Now it takes minutes. I think within a fairly short time, turning a group photo into a printable keepsake will feel as natural as printing a photo used to. We're not fully there yet, but we're clearly on that path.

r002.rationale: It describes group reconstruction as difficult, with face and identity errors, and says larger or occluded groups still need improvement or manual cleanup.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd say we're not there yet, and I want to be candid about that rather than oversell it.

Single-subject work is where Meshy is strong today. Give us one clear photo of a person or an object, and the model can produce a clean, watertight mesh that you can send to a printer with very little cleanup. That pipeline has matured a lot over the past couple of years.

Group photos are a different problem, and they're hard for a few reasons. First, occlusion. In a photo of five people, someone's arm is always in front of someone else's torso, and the model has to hallucinate what's hidden. For a single person, we can lean on strong priors about human anatomy. For a group, those priors interact, and the errors compound. Second, scale and depth. A 2D photo flattens the scene, so figuring out who's standing slightly behind whom, and how big each person actually is, is ambiguous. If you get that wrong, the printed result looks off even if every individual figure is fine. Third, the printing constraints themselves. A group scene has thin connections, gaps between people, and overhangs that a printer hates. Making it printable isn't just about geometry quality, it's about structural sanity.

So where we are right now is roughly this: we can segment a group photo, reconstruct each person reasonably well, and reassemble them into a scene. But the assembly step still needs human judgment, and the fine details, hands, faces, clothing folds, degrade noticeably compared to the single-subject case. A hobbyist who's willing to do some touch-up in Blender can get something nice. A consumer who wants to press one button and get a family figurine? We're not reliably there.

The good news is that the gap is closing fast. Multi-view and video input help enormously, because the occlusion problem largely goes away when you have a few angles. And the generative models are getting much better at consistent identity across figures. My guess is that within a year or two, the one-button family figurine becomes a real product rather than a demo. But I'd rather tell people where the rough edges are now than have them disappointed by a print.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts single-subject work with group photos, but never identifies individual game characters as a typical current use case.

r002.rationale: It describes single-person reconstruction as strong and says individual people can be reconstructed reasonably well; the stated shortcomings concern group assembly and fine details, not a general struggle to reconstruct humans.

astra-6.text: I’d separate that into two challenges: reconstructing the people from the photo and making the result printable. With a group photo, people can overlap, and the image doesn’t show their backs or other hidden details, so the model has to infer a lot. Then you need to make sure the geometry is connected and that thin parts can survive printing. I wouldn’t promise a faithful, print-ready model from any group photo in one click. Without a specific example to assess, I’d be cautious about claiming how well Meshy handles that today.

r001.rationale: The response discusses group-photo reconstruction and printability but does not identify individual game characters as a more typical Meshy use case.

r002.rationale: It notes challenges with occlusion, hidden details, and print-ready geometry, but does not state that Meshy still struggles to reconstruct humans well.

sol-6.1.text: I’d say it’s still a challenging use case. A group photo gives you only one view, and people often overlap, so the model has to infer a lot of geometry that isn’t visible. You might get something that captures the overall composition, but preserving each person’s likeness and producing a model that prints reliably are harder problems. I wouldn’t describe it as a dependable one-click workflow yet; you should expect to inspect the result and potentially do some cleanup before printing.
